title: Decode Your People: Using PCM to Build High-Performance Teams

all? I know it's quite loud. So, um, okay. Lucy was someone who lit up a room when she walked in. She was very warm, empathetic,
and really valued that connection. I clicked instantly with Lucy. Cam Cam was a bit different. Cam was very quiet, very analytical, data driven. He brought something very different to

of told myself, you know, that happens. Sometimes it just doesn't work out. But in reality, I knew deep down that as a manager, I had failed CAM.

model. And by the end of this talk, if you are managing a team, you will know who you've been speaking the wrong language to.
and more importantly what to do about it. So I want you to take a look at these stats gathered from both Gallup and Mercer

actively engaged and this is globally. What happens when you've got employees that are disengaged, have nowhere to turn, stressed anxious even a bit lost.
It learns, it leans towards burnout. And Mercer's most recent study shows that 82% of people in the workforce are showing signs of burnout. Now these are not abstract numbers.
These are your Lucy's. These are your CAMS. And as managers without any sort of formal training, we manage by instinct. We manage the way we like to be managed.
And that that is such a core part to why this is so important. I want to ask you a question. Can anybody raise their hand
if they've had somebody in their team that they ju they just have not been able to connect with? Someone that they've tried everything given as much support
as they possibly could. really believed in the person, but for some reason that distance just kept growing and growing and growing. I know I have.
And that's okay. You know, we make mistakes. We learn from them. But I want you to keep that person in mind throughout this talk. Okay? This
one is really for them. So I want to bring you back to the start of my of my story. We had Lucy who was
thriving and we had Cam who had left. Now why did I with two different people, different languages and my same management style get such different results?
And I asked myself this question time and time again and the answer for me was process communication model. Now this is not a personality test before
you start thinking it is. We're not putting people in boxes. We're not labeling others. We're talking about types in people, not types of people.
PCM is a way to decode human interaction. It was created by a American psychologist called Tabby Kaylor and it's come from decades of behavioral
research. Oh, excuse me. It gained international recognition through NASA in the 1970s. NASA used PCM in their hiring process for astronauts. They wanted to understand
who would be able to deal with highressured extreme environments and still stay calm. PCM is a framework that identifies six floors in your condominium.
We have the rebel floor, the imaginer floor, the promoter floor, the persist floor, the thinker floor, and the harmonizer floor. We have all six floors within us.
And the key thing that PCM does is that it helps you identify what is your ground floor which we call your base profile. Your base profile is your natural way of
being. It is the lens that you see the world through. It is how you communicate with others. It's what intrinsically motivates you. And it's what you do when
you fall under stress. PCM also identifies your phase which is the current floor that you are currently living in. Now if you're a manager and you're
wondering you know how to identify someone's base profile. Well there are three key ways to do that. The first is through informal language or natural language. The words
and phrases someone naturally uses whether it be around the lunch table, the dinner table, even on Slack. The second is communication style. Does someone enjoy speaking using lists
or data? Do they want to focus on developing a more personal connection? Do they enjoy sharing beliefs or opinions or do they do that regularly?
The fourth or sorry, the third is our stress behaviors and this is the most accurate way to identify someone's base profile. How someone acts when they fall into
distress is a clear indication of someone's base profile. Is somebody overcontrolling when they start falling into distress? Do they start overleasing? Do they withdraw
or do they start blaming or manipulating others? The fourth I have on this is motivation. Motivation can shift based on the phase that you are in. So yes, we all have an
intrinsic motivation, but it can change. For example, if you get your first ever job out of college based on if you're about to start a
family, very very different when it comes to your motivations. So today I want to analyze and go through two profiles. The first is going
to be the harmonizer floor. And this floor, somebody living on this floor is somebody that sees the world through emotions. They're very compassionate, sensitive,
warm individuals. Their psychological need is recognition of person. They value connection and relationships above everything else. They use words such as I feel. They
might start meetings with how are you doing today? Focusing on the person. This is actually my base profile. So a lot of this is very familiar to me.
I want to ask if you can raise your hand if you notice any of this in you or in your team quite a lot in the audience.
So what happens when someone with this base profile falls into distress? We start noticing patterns. The first pattern you will notice is somebody making very basic mistakes.
They're not able to focus properly. Then you'll notice they will start to overpleas. They will start to say yes when they actually mean no.
They will start to absorb everybody else's problems and put them above their own. Slowly but surely, this leads to a silent burnout. Now, if you are a manager and you have
somebody in your team and you're starting to notice these signs, you need to go to them. Don't wait for them to come to you
because they won't. You need to create a safe space for them to be able to share how they're feeling. And as a manager, you need to recognize
and support them. The best way to get somebody out of distress that's in this profile is by developing further trust and a deeper relationship.
The second profile I want to go through is our imaginerbased profile. Now this profile, somebody with this profile sees the world through reflection. They're very reflective, imaginative,
very calm, and actually very quiet individuals as well. Their psychological need is solitude. They value their space and their time and they will use words such as I
imagine, I reflect, picture this, I visualize this. Now, if you have does anybody see any of this inside of them or if they have any
team members with this type of profile, raise your hand. It's very common. So someone with this base profile, if you not start noticing signs of distress,
you will see their walls go up. They will start to go quiet and they will start to withdraw. It may look like disengagement, but it's
not. Now, if you're a manager and you start seeing these signs, do not do what I did. I added more meetings, added more support, more presence, more
collaboration. This only pushes this person further and further away. What they actually need is space time frame and trust that they will get the job done.
So now you know what a harmonizer base profile and an imaginerbased profile actually looks like. I want to bring you back to the story that I told you about
Lucy and Cam and I want to tell you what actually was happening there. So, as I mentioned, Lucy was warm empathetic. I knew she was going to be something
special. Our connection was natural. It was instant and it was easy. Like why was it so easy? Because my base profile was the same as
her base profile. So I didn't have to do anything different to what I would expect from a manager. On the other side, we had Cam.
Cam was very quiet, reflective. He brought something different to the team and I was so excited to have him on this team. But without me even knowing,
I was inputting my management style, which was a harmonizer base on CAM. And what did that do? That meant that I was adding more
meetings, more collaboration, more presence. Now, somebody with an imaginarybased profile, what do you think happens here? They fall into distress. They start to withdraw.
And as a manager, I noticed this. Of course, as I noticed this, this sends me into distress. So, I start overleasing. I started adding daily check-ins. I
started inviting him to the office more for more presence, more collaboration. My god, I absolutely suffocated the man. And of course, of course, he left.
Now can I ask has anybody been in that a situation just like Cam where you have not been able to get through you've added your needs your
communication style. It's very natural for us to do this as managers. So based on everything that I've said, what would have been the best way to manage
can? Give him space, give him time and trust that he will get that done. So with Lucy and Cam, we had two different people, two
different languages. And the most important thing for a manager is to be able to speak both. Here is exactly what actually had happened. I was applying my own needs, my own
language, not because I didn't care, but because I just didn't know any other way. And for me, PCM closed that gap. I didn't change my management style.
PCM gave me awareness and understanding of others needs. And that is so so important for managers to be able to understand. Speaking both languages
